title: Validating a turbulence closure means plotting wall-unit profiles against DNS, and saying what the numbers can and cannot show
summary: Closure-versus-DNS figures all use wall units: mean velocity against distance from the wall on a log axis, with the viscous sublayer and log law as reference. The same few checks apply whether the figure shows a mean profile, an eddy-viscosity profile, a fitted coefficient, an error scorecard or a colour-coded anisotropy state.

media.alt: Two panels of U-plus against y-plus on a log x axis (1 to several thousand). Black dots are DNS data rising from about 1 to about 18 (left, Re-tau 180) and about 22.5 (right, Re-tau 1000), following a dotted log-law line at large y-plus. A purple model curve stays nearly flat near 1 in both panels. The title states a large disclosed miss against DNS.

read_the_figure.question: Does the closure's mean velocity profile follow the DNS across the sublayer, the buffer layer and the log layer, at both Reynolds numbers?
read_the_figure.axes: x: distance from the wall in wall units, y-plus (log scale). y: mean velocity in wall units, U-plus. Left panel: friction Reynolds number near 180; right panel: near 1000. Black dots are the reference DNS data; the dotted line is the analytic log law.
look_at: Start with the reference: dots follow U-plus = y-plus up to about y-plus = 5, bend through the buffer layer, then run parallel to the dotted line above about y-plus = 30. This is the shape every good closure must reproduce.
Check that the model curve starts at the same place as the DNS at y-plus of order 1. Here the model line is nearly horizontal, so it never develops a rise at all.
Compare the Reynolds numbers: the log region lengthens from the left to the right panel, and the DNS in the right panel reaches higher U-plus.
The dotted log law is analytic, not data. It is only expected to match above y-plus of about 30 and well below the channel centre.
Read the legend for the actual Reynolds number of the DNS (182 and 1001 here), which differs slightly from the nominal title.
The title carries a statement of failure. Treat the figure as a diagnostic of what is missing, not as a validation.
read_the_figure.proves: If the model curve lies on the DNS dots from the sublayer to the log region at both Reynolds numbers, the closure reproduces the mean profile for this flow. A mismatch like the one drawn proves only that this implementation does not yet do so; the cause needs separate tests.
if_wrong: A flat or constant model curve: the momentum equation is not being driven or not coupled to the stress model, or the solution did not converge. A single scalar error value would hide that.
A curve that matches near the wall but departs above: the outer-region model (length scale or dissipation) is wrong.
A good match at one Reynolds number only: the model has been tuned to that case; compare with a held-out case, as the data-driven figure does.
A good fit that comes with an eddy viscosity near zero: the stress balance is carried by the wrong term. Check the stress budget, as in the DES figure.
must_check: Same Reynolds number, same wall units, same domain (channel half-width) as the DNS.
The reference is data, not a formula, and its source is cited.
A force-balance or stress-balance check passes: it is necessary, but not sufficient for a good profile.
The error metric: which points (log spaced?), which norm, relative to what.
For a fitted correction, which Reynolds numbers were used to train it and which to test it.
as_drawn: DNS at the left Reynolds number: U-plus about 1 at y-plus 1, about 8 at y-plus 10, about 17 at y-plus 100, about 18 at the centreline.
DNS at the right Reynolds number: about 1 at y-plus 1, about 8 at 10, about 16.5 at 100, about 22.5 at y-plus 1000.
Dotted log law reads about 5.2 at y-plus 1; its slope, from the end of the left curve (17.9 at y-plus 180), is about 2.4 per unit of ln y-plus, i.e. a von Karman constant of about 0.41 (computed).
The model curve is about 1 over the whole range at both Reynolds numbers.

terms.meaning: Lengths and velocities scaled with the friction velocity and the kinematic viscosity, so that near-wall profiles collapse for different flows.
The channel half-width in wall units. It is also the ratio of outer to inner scale.

terms.term: Viscous sublayer, buffer layer, log layer
terms.meaning: The three near-wall regions of a turbulent boundary layer or channel: where viscosity dominates, where viscous and turbulent stresses compete, and where turbulent stress dominates.
The profile of the overlap region. kappa is the von Karman constant, B an additive constant.
The assumption that the turbulent shear stress is proportional to the mean shear. The factor is the eddy viscosity.
A model that solves transport equations for each Reynolds stress component instead of using an eddy viscosity.
The traceless part of the normalised Reynolds stress. Its invariants place the turbulence state in a triangle between one-component, two-component and isotropic limits.
A fitted correction is fitted on one set of cases and evaluated unchanged on another. The difference in error is the generalisation gap.

remember: Near the wall U-plus equals y-plus; far from it the log law with kappa about 0.41 and B about 5.2 holds (both consistent with the figure).
The total shear stress in a channel is a straight line in y: viscous plus turbulent stress equals u_tau squared times 1 minus y over h.
In local equilibrium in the log layer the Boussinesq model gives C_mu = (shear stress over k) squared, which for the textbook value is 0.09.
A force balance is satisfied by many wrong profiles; it checks the budget, not the shape.
An error scorecard compresses a table into colour, but cannot say why a cell is high.
A model fitted on one Reynolds number must be judged on another.

understand.title: One reference, many ways to fail
understand.text: Every figure of the group compares a model with the same DNS-based reference. A flat curve (stress-transport run), an eddy viscosity that collapses in the outer region (hybrid RANS-LES switch on a 1D grid), a fitted coefficient that does not transfer (train versus held-out), and a uniform bright stripe in a scorecard are four different failure signatures. The scorecard tells you which cell to look at; the profile tells you what is wrong.

understand.title: Why the project shows its misses
understand.text: A validation figure that fails is evidence about the method that created it. Showing the failure with its title and with the reference data lets the reader judge the size of the gap, and shows that the passing checks (such as a force balance) did not guarantee a good profile. Read the group in that spirit: as honest diagnostics.

understand.title: Anisotropy as colour
understand.text: The painting maps each wall-normal point to a position in the Lumley triangle and then to an RGB colour through barycentric weights. It is a legend, not a measurement: the colour is only as good as the Reynolds-stress state it comes from, and the wall point is excluded because its stress values are placeholders.

steps.title: Wall units
steps.note: Scaling by the friction velocity makes the near-wall region universal, so profiles at different Reynolds numbers share a common curve below y-plus of about 30.

steps.title: The stress balance of a channel
steps.note: Integrating the mean momentum equation for steady fully developed flow driven by a pressure gradient. In wall units: dU+/dy+ minus the turbulent stress equals 1 minus y over h. This single relation is why the wall layer has the shape it has.

steps.title: Sublayer and log layer
steps.note: Near the wall the turbulent stress vanishes and the balance gives U-plus = y-plus. Far from it the turbulent stress is the whole stress and dimensional analysis gives the logarithm. With B = 5.2 the log law reads 16.4 at y-plus 100.

steps.title: What an eddy-viscosity closure must reproduce
steps.note: Inverting the Boussinesq relation against DNS gives an implied C_mu at each wall distance. If the model's constant (0.09 in the textbook form) were correct, the implied curve would be flat. The data-driven figure plots exactly this implied curve.

steps.title: Local equilibrium and the 0.09
steps.note: In the log layer production equals dissipation, which ties C_mu to the ratio of shear stress to turbulent kinetic energy. A value of 0.09 corresponds to that ratio being 0.3. The DNS-implied plateau of C_mu can differ between Reynolds numbers, as the held-out curve shows.

steps.title: A hybrid length scale and why viscosity can collapse
steps.note: The switch replaces the wall distance by the grid spacing when the grid is coarse relative to the wall distance. On a 1D grid there are no resolved eddies to carry the stress, so removing the eddy viscosity leaves a laminar balance and U-plus grows without bound. That is why the DES panel's mean profile departs so strongly while the near-wall part agrees.

steps.title: Barycentric colours from the anisotropy tensor
steps.note: Eigenvalues of b_ij in descending order, which sum to zero. The three weights are the one-component, two-component and isotropic fractions, and they sum to one because the trace is zero. For b = diag(2/3, -1/3, -1/3) the weights are 1, 0, 0 (one-component limit); for b = 0 they are 0, 0, 1 (isotropic).

steps.title: An RMS relative error
steps.note: A scorecard cell reports a number of this kind. Its value depends on which points are sampled and on relative weighting: a model that is exact in the log layer but wrong near the wall is penalised differently from the reverse. Colour scales capped at 100 percent keep one large cell from flattening the rest.

worked.title: Log law at y-plus 100 against the DNS dots
worked.problem: With kappa = 0.41 and B = 5.2, what U-plus does the log law give at y-plus 100? The DNS dots at that point read about 17. How large is the difference?
worked.answer: The log law gives about 16.4, within about 4 percent of the DNS dots at this point (values read by eye), which is why the dotted line is a fair reference in the overlap region.

analyze.q: The model curve in the representative figure is nearly constant at about 1. List three causes that would give a flat curve and the cheapest test for each.
analyze.hint: Check the driving term, the coupling between stress and momentum, and the convergence history.

analyze.q: The DNS-implied C_mu plateaus at different values for the two Reynolds numbers, and neither equals the textbook constant. What does that imply for a single constant and for a single-Reynolds-number fit?
analyze.hint: The log layer is short at the lower Reynolds number.

analyze.q: In the DES panel the near-wall profiles agree and the outer ones do not. Which part of the formula for the length scale explains that, and why can a 1D grid not test the hybrid idea?
analyze.hint: The minimum of two lengths; no resolved eddies in a 1D domain.

evaluate.q: A closure passes a force-balance regression and fails a profile comparison. Which result should be believed, and what should be reported?
evaluate.hint: One is necessary, the other is the goal.

evaluate.q: Is a scorecard with a single number per cell enough to rank closures? What would you add?
evaluate.hint: Point sampling, uncertainty and the failure mode.

create: Add to the profile figure a third panel with the relative error against y-plus, on the same log axis, so the reader sees where the error accumulates rather than one number.
Design a train and test protocol for a fitted correction using three Reynolds numbers: which one is held out and what is reported.

checks.q: Why are profiles plotted in wall units on a logarithmic y-plus axis?
checks.hint: What collapses and what is magnified?
checks.answer: Wall units make near-wall profiles universal across flows and Reynolds numbers, and the log axis spreads out the thin region near the wall where most of the structure is while turning the log law into a straight line.

checks.q: What U-plus does the log law (kappa 0.41, B 5.2) give at y-plus 50?
checks.answer: ln 50 = 3.912, divided by 0.41 is 9.54, plus 5.2 is 14.7.

checks.q: Why does removing the eddy viscosity in the outer region make U-plus grow so strongly?
checks.answer: The total stress is fixed by the momentum balance. With the turbulent contribution gone the whole stress must be carried by the viscous term, so the gradient dU/dy equals u_tau squared times 1 minus y over h over nu, which is large, and the integrated velocity becomes very large.

checks.q: A fitted correction matches its training Reynolds number well but not a held-out one. Is the fit useless?
checks.hint: What did you learn about the fit?
checks.answer: It is useful as a finding: it shows the fit encodes features specific to the training case and that more Reynolds numbers or a physically motivated form are needed. It is not useful as a general closure. The honest report states both the training and the held-out error.

checks.q: How would you design a colour legend for the Lumley triangle that stays readable for colour-blind readers?
checks.hint: The barycentric weights are three numbers summing to one.
checks.answer: Keep the barycentric RGB for the ribbon but also label the corners with text, add a small triangular key, and offer a luminance-only version in which the one-component weight maps to dark and the isotropic weight to light. A direct plot of the three weights against y gives the same information without relying on colour alone.
